front: [Chain: RFQ_WIN 1/4] Context: a real-money client sells £50m nominal of a 10y gilt on a D2C RFQ platform (Tradeweb or Bloomberg) and asks five dealers to quote. Your bid is the best of the five. Define the hit ratio, and say what a win tells you about your price beyond your own P&L.
back:
Hit ratio = wins / quotes shown, count-based and also notional-weighted. Example: 150 wins from 1,000 quotes in a week is a 15% hit ratio.
What a win tells you: the client chose you because your bid was the best of the five. Your bid is your own fair-value estimate less your spread, so a win is selected evidence: your estimate was the highest of the five estimates. It is not an independent observation of the market.
Desk use: track hit ratio by client, size band, tier and time of day. A falling hit ratio at a stable price usually means a competitor has moved tighter, or your estimate has drifted from the others.
Interviewer follow-up: is a high hit ratio good? Not by itself. Card 3 shows a tight quote can win often and still lose money.

front: [Chain: RFQ_WIN 2/4] Context: the same five-dealer RFQ. Each dealer's fair-yield estimate has independent error with standard deviation \(\sigma = 0.5\)bp, and each dealer bids its estimate less a fixed spread. Conditional on winning, what is the expected error in your estimate, and what does it cost you in yield and in £ at DV01 £40k/bp?
back:
Winning means your estimate is the maximum of all five dealers' estimates, yours included.
\(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{us}\mid\text{win}] = \sigma\,\mathbb{E}\big[\max_{i\le 5} Z_i\big]\), with \(Z_i\) iid standard normal.
\(\mathbb{E}[\max_{i\le 5} Z_i]\approx 1.163\) (for comparison \(k=2\): 0.564, \(k=3\): 0.846, \(k=4\): 1.029). So the conditional error is \(0.5\times1.163\approx 0.58\)bp.
Monte Carlo check (400,000 draws): mean error given a win is 0.58bp, and the win frequency is 20% (1 in 5 by symmetry).
Cost: you buy the bonds about 0.58bp of yield richer than the average dealer's fair value. At DV01 £40k/bp that is about £23k per win.
Interviewer follow-up: why does the curse grow with the number of dealers? Because \(\mathbb{E}[\max]\) rises with \(k\), so five dealers (1.16\(\sigma\)) costs more than three (0.85\(\sigma\)).

front: [Chain: RFQ_WIN 3/4] Context: you quote a 1.0bp yield edge over your fair value, so the gross edge is 1.0bp. The winner's curse from the previous card is 0.51bp. DV01 is £40k/bp per £50m trade, and hedging costs £5k per trade. Work out the net P&L per win and per week at 150 wins, and what happens if you tighten to a 0.5bp edge to raise the hit ratio.
back:
Net edge = 1.0 − 0.58 = 0.42bp (0.418 before rounding).
Gross per win = 0.418bp × £40,000/bp ≈ £16,700.
After hedging = £16,700 − £5,000 ≈ £11,700 per win.
Week = 150 × £11,740 ≈ £1.76m.
Sanity check: 150 trades carry 150 × £40k = £6m of DV01 traded. £1.76m / £6m = 0.29bp per unit of DV01 traded, which equals 0.418 − 5,000/40,000 = 0.293bp. Consistent.
Tightening to 0.5bp: net edge ≈ 0.5 − 0.58 = −0.08bp. Each win loses about £3,300 before the £5k hedge cost. The hit ratio rises, the P&L falls. The winner's curse makes the spread you can afford wider than the gross edge you think you have.
Interviewer follow-up: what would make 0.5bp viable? Lower σ (better estimates) or a smaller field of dealers. Both cut \(\mathbb{E}[\max]\sigma\).

front: [Chain: RFQ_WIN 4/4] Context: over the last month, your 5-minute dealer markout on quotes you won averages −0.6bp, while the markout on all quotes you responded to averages −0.1bp. Explain what the gap means, how you would confirm it, and two changes you would make to the quoting rule.
back:
Meaning: the gap is the signature of the winner's curse. Winning selects quotes where your estimate was high in the direction that costs you, so the post-trade mid moves against you more after wins than on average.
Confirm: split by outcome (won vs lost quotes), by size band, and by client. Use the lost quotes as a control: the move in the mid after a lost quote shows the market drift you would have had without selection. Check the gap is not explained by a single event window (a data release or auction) that sits in the sample.
Change 1: add a curse term to the quote: the spread on bucket \(b\) is \(h_b = h_0 + k\,\hat\sigma_b\,\mathbb{E}[\max_{i\le n}Z_i]\), with \(\hat\sigma_b\) the estimated estimate error for that bucket and \(n\) the expected number of dealers.
Change 2: reprice clients by their win-conditional markout, not the average. A client that asks five dealers every time generates more curse than one that asks two, so their spread should carry a higher curse term.
Where it breaks: a win-conditional markout can also reflect genuine client information. You need enough wins per bucket to separate the two effects, otherwise the curse term is fitted to noise.

front: Derivation: A dealer quotes a half-spread \(h\) (bp) over its fair estimate. It wins with probability \(p(h)=1/(1+e^{(h-h_0)/s})\), a logistic hit curve. Conditional on winning, the adverse-selection cost is \(a\) bp (the winner's curse). Find the \(h\) that maximises expected P&L per RFQ, and evaluate it for \(a=0.5\), \(h_0=1.5\), \(s=0.3\) (bp).
back:
Objective: \(V(h)=(h-a)\,p(h)\).
Logistic derivative: \(p'(h)=-\dfrac{p(h)\,(1-p(h))}{s}\).
First-order condition: \(V'(h)=p+(h-a)p'=p\Big[1-\dfrac{(h-a)(1-p)}{s}\Big]=0\), so \(h^*=a+\dfrac{s}{1-p^*}\).
Numbers (python grid, step 0.001bp): \(h^*=1.33\)bp, \(p^*=0.638\), \(V^*=0.53\)bp per RFQ. Check: \(0.5+0.3/0.362=1.329\).
Comparison: at \(h=1.0\)bp, \(V=0.42\); at \(h=1.5\)bp, \(V=0.50\); at \(h=2.0\)bp, \(V=0.24\). The optimum is not the tightest spread that wins often, nor the widest that wins rarely.
Interviewer follow-up: what does the first-order condition say about the hit ratio at the optimum? \(p^*\) is set by \(s\) and \(a\): a noisier hit curve (larger \(s\)) raises the optimal hit ratio and widens the optimal spread.
Where it breaks: the hit curve is not a fixed function of your spread. You face the best of the competitors' quotes, so \(p\) depends on the competitor distribution. Also \(a\) rises as \(h\) falls, because a lower hit ratio comes with more informed winners. With \(a=a(h)\) the condition becomes \(p+(h-a(h))p'-a'(h)p=0\).

front: Derivation: A gilt quote is given in yield but traded in price. Derive the change in clean price for a yield change \(\Delta y\), and evaluate a 0.2bp yield half-spread on a 10y gilt at par with modified duration 8.0, on a £50m trade.
back:
Taylor expansion of the clean price \(P(y)\): \(\Delta P = P'(y)\Delta y+\tfrac12 P''(y)\Delta y^2\).
With \(P'(y)=-D_{mod}P\) and \(P''(y)=C\,P\), where \(C\) is convexity in years squared: \(\Delta P\approx -D_{mod}P\,\Delta y+\tfrac12 C P\,\Delta y^2\).
Numbers: \(\Delta y=0.2\)bp \(=2\times10^{-5}\), \(D_{mod}=8.0\), \(P=100\). First term: \(-8.0\times100\times2\times10^{-5}=-0.016\) price points per £100 nominal. Convexity term with \(C\approx 90\): \(\tfrac12\times90\times100\times(2\times10^{-5})^2=1.8\times10^{-6}\), negligible.
Sanity: 0.016 points on £50m is 0.016% of £50m = £8,000, which equals £40k/bp × 0.2bp. Consistent.
Sign: price and yield move oppositely, so a higher price is a lower yield. Convert each side of the market separately: the dealer's price offer maps to a yield below mid, and the spread is set on the side the client pays. Never add a yield half-spread to a price directly.
Where it breaks: for large \(\Delta y\) the convexity term matters, and the sign flip is easy to get wrong on the offer side. Quote on clean price, because accrued interest does not move with yield.

front: Derivation: A long gilt future delivers a basket, and the cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) bond is held fixed for the purpose of the hedge. The futures price is \(F=(P_{CTD}-\text{PV(coupons)})/CF\). Show that the futures DV01 is \(\mathrm{DV01}_{CTD}/CF\), and compute how many contracts hedge a £200m 10y receive-fixed swap (book DV01 \(\approx\)£166k/bp) when the CTD has modified duration 8.0 and conversion factor 0.85.
back:
Step 1: Holding the CTD and the coupon PV fixed, \(\Delta F\approx \Delta P_{CTD}/CF\), so \(\mathrm{DV01}_F=\mathrm{DV01}_{CTD}/CF\), where DV01 is per contract on the deliverable face.
Step 2: per £100k of CTD face, \(\mathrm{DV01}=100{,}000\times8.0\times10^{-4}=\pounds80\)/bp. So \(\mathrm{DV01}_F=80/0.85=\pounds94.1\)/bp per contract.
Step 3: book DV01 = \(200\text{m}\times8.3\times10^{-4}\approx\pounds166{,}000\)/bp (\(D_{mod}\approx8.3\) for the swap). Contracts \(N=166{,}000/94.1\approx1{,}764\).
Direction: receiving fixed makes you long duration, so sell about 1,764 contracts.
Sanity: 1,764 × £94.1 ≈ £166k/bp.
Where it breaks: (i) the CTD can switch, which changes \(\mathrm{DV01}_F\) discontinuously; (ii) the conversion factor is fixed at a notional yield, so the hedge is exact only near that yield; (iii) futures versus cash basis is not captured by DV01 matching.
Interviewer follow-up: what if the CTD DV01 falls by 10% (say a new CTD)? The contract count falls by 10% for the same book, and the hedge is wrong by 10% of the book DV01 until rebalanced.

front: Derivation: A dealer sells £50m of 10y gilts to a client. With probability \(\pi\) the client is informed and the mid then moves \(m\) bp against the dealer. Otherwise the mid does not move. The dealer charges a half-spread \(h\) bp. Derive the expected dealer P&L per trade and the breakeven \(h\). Evaluate for \(\pi=0.3\) and \(m=2\)bp.
back:
Expected P&L: uninformed client: P&L = \(h\). Informed client: P&L = \(h-m\). So \(\mathbb{E}[\text{P\&L}]=(1-\pi)h+\pi(h-m)=h-\pi m\).
Breakeven: \(h^*=\pi m\). Numbers: \(h^*=0.3\times2=0.6\)bp.
At \(h=1.0\)bp: expected P&L \(=0.4\)bp per trade, which is £16,000 at DV01 £40k/bp (\(0.4\times40{,}000\)).
Reading: the dealer cannot see which client is informed, so the measured average markout equals \(-\pi m\). A desk that reports a 0.6bp average markout is seeing \(\pi=0.3\) with \(m=2\), or \(\pi=0.15\) with \(m=4\). The two cases need different responses.
Interviewer follow-up: how would you estimate \(\pi\) per client? Use the realised markout distribution by client over a rolling window, with a confidence interval, not a point estimate.
Where it breaks: part of the post-trade move is your own hedging impact, not information. Also \(m\) is size dependent, and a skewed quote changes \(\pi\) because it changes which clients trade.

front: [Chain: MARK 1/3] Context: a dealer sells £50m of a 10y gilt to a client at a yield of 4.190%. The mid at the trade is 4.200%. Five minutes later the mid is 4.185%. DV01 is £40k/bp. Define effective spread, markout and realised spread from the dealer's side, and compute each in bp and in £.
back:
Effective spread (dealer edge at the trade): the dealer sells at a yield 1.0bp below mid, so it sells above fair price and earns the spread: \(4.200-4.190=+1.0\)bp, which is £40,000.
Markout (the mid's move after the trade, in the dealer's P&L sign): the dealer is now short the bond. Yields fell 1.5bp, prices rose, and the short loses: \(-1.5\)bp, which is −£60,000.
Realised spread = effective spread + markout = \(1.0+(-1.5)=-0.5\)bp, which is −£20,000. After five minutes the dealer is out of the money on the trade.
Convention: every markout in this chain is in dealer P&L terms: negative means the mid moved against the dealer.
Interviewer follow-up: which mid is 4.200%? The mid used in the trade-time reference, from a composite or your own curve. Card 3 covers how this choice moves the answer.

front: [Chain: MARK 2/3] Context: a month of gilt RFQ flow split into three client tiers. Average effective spread (dealer edge, bp): tier A real money 1.0; tier B fast hedge-fund flow 1.5; tier C corporate and insurance 1.2. Average 5-minute markout (dealer P&L, bp): A −0.3, B −1.2, C −0.4. Which tier earns the desk the most per unit of risk, and why is the widest-spread tier not the best one?
back:
Realised spread per tier = effective + markout: A +0.7bp, B +0.3bp, C +0.8bp.
Reading: tier B quotes the widest spread (1.5bp) but keeps the least: 1.2bp of its edge is given back to informed flow within five minutes. Tier C earns the largest realised spread in bp, at 0.8bp, but tier A keeps 70% of its spread (0.7 of 1.0) against 67% for tier C (0.8 of 1.2).
Metric: optimise realised spread weighted by DV01 traded, not the quoted effective spread. Tier A at 0.7bp on the largest DV01 is the franchise. Tier C's realised spread is best, but on the smallest DV01.
Action: reprice B first, by widening or capping size, unless its volume is needed for cross-product or hedging value. Cutting spread on A to win more volume is a bet on elasticity you have not measured.
Interviewer follow-up: is 5 minutes the right horizon? Not necessarily. The next card shows how the horizon changes the story.

front: [Chain: MARK 3/3] Context: tier B's markout is −0.2bp at one second and −1.2bp at five minutes. Tier A's markout is −0.1bp at one second and −0.3bp at five minutes. Explain what the shape of the markout curve tells you, and list four ways the measurement itself can be wrong.
back:
Shape: a markout that grows with the horizon means the market moved after the trade in the direction the client expected, so the client's flow carried information. Tier B's curve grows from 0.2 to 1.2bp, which is informed flow. A markout that reverts means the dealer's own trade pushed the price temporarily (inventory or liquidity cost), which is a different fix: a hedging or pricing problem, not a client problem.
Measurement failures:
  • Mid definition: your own quote mid, a stale indicative, or a single-venue mid carries its own bounce. Use a consistent composite and record which one.
  • Event windows: a scheduled data release or an auction inside the five minutes contaminates the number. Flag and exclude, or report separately.
  • Selection: markouts computed only on accepted trades hide the flow you rejected. If last look rejects adverse fills, the accepted-trade markout understates the adverse flow.
  • Double counting: a hedge fill inside the window must not be booked as a client trade, or the markout includes your own hedge impact twice.
Interviewer follow-up: what is the control? The same-direction market move over the same window, measured on comparable quotes that were not traded.

front: [Chain: AUTOHEDGE 1/3] Context: a client pays fixed on £200m of 10y swaps, so you receive fixed and are long duration. Swap modified duration is 8.3, so book DV01 is about £166k/bp. The hedge is 10y gilt futures with DV01 £94.1/bp per contract (CTD modified duration 8.0, conversion factor 0.85). A half-tick of execution cost is about £5 per contract per side. Give the hedge size, the one-side cost, and the decision: hedge immediately or warehouse.
back:
Size: 166,000 / 94.1 ≈ 1,764 contracts, sold to hedge the receive-fixed exposure.
One-side cost: 1,764 × £5 ≈ £8,800.
Risk being hedged: an assumed 1-day 1σ move of 5bp on the 10y gives £166k × 5 ≈ £830,000. The hedge cost is about 1% of one day's 1σ risk.
Decision: at that ratio the question is not whether to hedge the full DV01 but how fast. Immediate hedging of the full DV01 is the default, unless the desk has an explicit warehouse mandate with a measured expected reversion or flow-netting value.
Interviewer follow-up: what if the book is already long £400k/bp? Then hedge the net, not the new trade. Adding a receiver against an existing long DV01 may need no hedge at all, and the trade's marginal cost is its change in net DV01.
Note: the £94.1 and the 5bp are illustrative assumptions; the rule is the same with any contract DV01 or volatility.

front: [Chain: AUTOHEDGE 2/3] Context: same £200m swap, but the desk's rule is to warehouse up to £100k/bp of residual DV01 per bucket and hedge the excess immediately. Compute the hedge, the one-side cost, and the residual 1-day 1σ risk. State the trade-off that sets the £100k threshold.
back:
Excess: £166k − £100k = £66k/bp. Contracts: 66,000 / 94.1 ≈ 701.
One-side cost: 701 × £5 ≈ £3,500.
Residual risk: £100k/bp × 5bp = £500,000 of 1-day 1σ, down from £830,000.
Trade-off: the warehouse saves about £3,500 on this trade and in return carries about £330,000 of extra 1-day 1σ risk (£830k − £500k). The threshold is set by (a) the risk limit the desk is allowed, (b) the measured expected value of waiting (reversion, netting with flow that will arrive, a better hedge price), and (c) the cost of rebalancing when the warehoused DV01 grows. A warehouse with no measured expected value is a risk position, not a hedge decision.
Where it breaks: a single DV01 threshold ignores curve shape. £100k in the 2y bucket and £100k in the 30y bucket carry very different curve risk, so the threshold should be bucketed.

front: [Chain: AUTOHEDGE 3/3] Context: the hedge is on, and the swap-to-futures basis (the spread between the swap and the hedge instrument) moves 0.5bp against you. Separately, the auto-hedger rebalances whenever residual DV01 exceeds £10k/bp, and its DV01 estimate is noisy. Quantify the basis loss on the full £166k/bp book, and name the two failure modes that cause repeated hedging.
back:
Basis loss: £166k × 0.5bp ≈ £83,000. A DV01 hedge does not remove basis risk. It is residual P&L.
Failure mode 1, whipsaw: a noisy DV01 estimate, or a DV01 that moves with curve shape, crosses the £10k/bp trigger in both directions. Each round trip of 1,764 contracts costs about 1,764 × £5 × 2 ≈ £17,600 in half-ticks, plus the time to fill.
Failure mode 2, CTD switch: the futures DV01 jumps when the cheapest-to-deliver changes, so the hedge is re-sized in one step with a large fill.
Fix: use hysteresis (hedge when the residual exceeds an upper band, unwind only below a lower band), use a CTD-aware DV01 with a smoothed estimate, and hedge the curve in buckets rather than aggregate DV01.
Interviewer follow-up: how do you size the bands? From the expected cost of a round trip against the expected cost of carrying the residual for the time it takes the noise to resolve.

front: Case study: monthly gilt RFQ P&L by client tier, in £. Notional traded in the month, all 10y gilts at modified duration 8.0: tier A £2.4bn, tier B £0.9bn, tier C £0.3bn. Average effective spreads and 5-minute markouts (dealer P&L, bp): A 1.0 and −0.3; B 1.5 and −1.2; C 1.2 and −0.4. Compute the DV01 traded per tier, the gross effective P&L, the markout P&L, and the realised P&L in £ and DV01-weighted bp. Say which tier to reprice first.
back:
DV01 traded = notional × 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ per £: A £1.92m/bp, B £0.72m/bp, C £0.24m/bp, total £2.88m/bp.
Effective P&L (spread × DV01): A 1.0 × 1.92 = £1.92m; B 1.5 × 0.72 = £1.08m; C 1.2 × 0.24 = £0.288m. Total £3.288m.
Markout P&L: A −0.3 × 1.92 = −£0.576m; B −1.2 × 0.72 = −£0.864m; C −0.4 × 0.24 = −£0.096m. Total −£1.536m.
Realised P&L: A £1.344m; B £0.216m; C £0.192m. Total £1.752m.
DV01-weighted realised spread: 1.752 / 2.88 ≈ 0.61bp.
Sanity: total effective − total markout = 3.288 − 1.536 = 1.752, matching the sum of tier realised P&L.
Reprice first: tier B. Its markout is four times tier A's per unit of DV01 (−1.2 against −0.3), and its realised spread is the lowest at 0.3bp. Before cutting, check whether B's flow is a hedging or cross-product feed and what its volume would do at a wider quote. Costs (hedge, fees, funding) are excluded here.
Interviewer follow-up: what does 2.88m/bp of DV01 traded mean? A parallel 1bp move across all the month's trades is a £2.88m gross exposure. It is not a risk position, but it sets the scale of the spread income.

front: Case study: what a 250ms feed lag costs a streaming gilt quote. Assume a 10y gilt daily 1σ of 5bp (illustrative), an 8.5-hour trading day, and DV01 of £40k/bp on the quote. Your quote is stale by 250ms. Compute the 1σ mid move during the lag in bp and £, then the expected adverse cost per quote if a client takes the quote only when it is stale in its favour. State the scaling with latency and where the calculation breaks.
back:
Intraday σ: σ per √second = 5 / √(8.5 × 3,600) = 5 / √30,600 ≈ 0.0286bp.
Move during 0.25s: σ × √0.25 = 0.0286 × 0.5 ≈ 0.0143bp, which at £40k/bp is about £572 (1σ).
Expected adverse if taken only when favourable: for a normal move \(X\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(\mathbb{E}[\max(X,0)]=\sigma/\sqrt{2\pi}\approx0.399\sigma\). So the expected cost per stale fill is 0.399 × £572 ≈ £228. A thousand such fills a day cost about £228k.
Scaling: cost per quote scales with \(\sqrt{\text{latency}}\), not linearly. A tenfold latency increase raises the per-quote cost by about 3.2 times (\(\sqrt{10}\)). Defensive quoting therefore widens by \(k\,\sigma\sqrt{\tau}\) and cuts size after a staleness timer, rather than assuming cost is proportional to delay.
Where it breaks: intraday volatility is not uniform. It is higher at scheduled releases and at the open, so \(\sqrt{\tau}\) with a flat σ understates stale-quote cost at those times. The 'always adverse' selection is also an upper bound. Real flow picks off only a fraction of stale quotes.

front: Scenario: It is 07:15. You are short £400k/bp of 10y gilt DV01 from yesterday's client flow. Overnight the US 10y is 4bp higher, but your gilt mid is still the 16:30 close from yesterday and no gilt trade has printed since. A scheduled UK data release at 07:00 has just come out. Walk through what you do before the open of the cash market, with numbers.
back:
1. Do not mark on the stale close. Re-mark on a composite mid from the early session, or from the futures-implied level, and record the mid source. Stale marks are the commonest source of morning P&L surprises.
2. Attribute the overnight move. A 60-day beta of gilts to USTs of about 0.5 (illustrative) implies the 10y gilt should be about +2bp. If the observed gilt move is 0, the gap is 2bp, which on £400k/bp is £800k of potential mark. Check whether the gap is an artefact of the stale mid or a real divergence.
3. Check the release. Read the print against consensus and check the reaction in breakevens and front-end before deciding whether the overnight UST move is the whole story.
4. Check queued flow and limits. Look at open RFQs, the axe, and DV01 usage against the bucket limit. If the book is near limit, decide the hedge now, not after the open.
5. Decide. A short gilt position gains when yields rise, so an implied 2bp sell-off is roughly £800k in the desk's favour on re-marking; do not hedge that gain. Hedge only if the book is at its limit or the release could reverse the move, and then hedge the excess with futures before the cash open. If the gap is a stale mid, correct the mark and keep the position.
Interviewer follow-up: when would you hedge a move that is in your favour? When the book is at its DV01 limit, or when the release could reverse the expected move. Both must be measured, not assumed.

front: Scenario: It is 16:15. The P&L explain on a £400k/bp 10y gilt book shows £180k unexplained, with no large new trades and no curve bucket outside the 10y. Walk through how you find the break, using the numbers.
back:
1. Split the explain by source: new trades (booking versus pricing curve), carry and roll, curve bucket moves, volatility and convexity, and theta. Locate which source holds the £180k.
2. Divide by DV01: £180k / £400k per bp = 0.45bp. The unexplained P&L equals a 0.45bp move on the whole book. A 0.45bp residual on one bucket points to a level mismatch: the pricing yield and the mark are off by that much.
3. Test for a single trade: £180k / £40k per bp = 4.5bp. A single £50m trade priced 4.5bp off the right level, or booked at a stale price, produces exactly this kind of number. Check the largest trades of the day against their own pricing.
4. Check conventions: clean versus dirty price, settlement date, accrued interest at a coupon date, and whether the pricing curve uses the same bootstrap as the mark.
5. Check the curve: compare yesterday's and today's pricing curves node by node, to see whether the change is in the market or in the bootstrap.
Control angle: an unexplained P&L above the desk threshold goes to product control with the bucket split, the trade list checked, and the source identified. It is not explained away as 'noise' at 16:15.
Interviewer follow-up: why does a 4.5bp single-trade pattern matter more than a 0.45bp book-wide one? The first is a booking or pricing error to find; the second is more likely a curve mismatch affecting the whole book.

front: Scenario: It is 13:05. A tier-1 real-money client sends a D2C RFQ to five dealers for £100m of 10y gilts, asking to buy from the dealers. You are already short £60m (DV01 about −£48k/bp). Give your quote logic, your hedge, and the inventory consequence. Use the numbers from the desk's model: DV01 £80k/bp per £100m, futures DV01 £94.1/bp per contract.
back:
Inventory after the trade: you sell £100m more, so the short becomes £160m, with DV01 −£128k/bp (the existing −£48k plus −£80k).
Hedge: the new £80k/bp is hedged by buying about 80,000 / 94.1 ≈ 850 futures contracts. Doing it immediately is the default, unless the position is part of a measured warehouse.
Quote: you are short, so you want to reduce the short. Skew the quote: tighten the side that would buy bonds from the client, and widen the side that sells more. For a client buying from you, that means your offer is the one you widen. Keep the total spread to the tier-1 level, not the level the inventory alone would demand, because an unskewed quote wins less often and an over-skewed quote loses the client.
Check before quoting: the tier's realised spread net of markout (see the markout chain) and the win-conditional markout on this client. A tier-1 client with a low realised spread can justify a tight quote, but only if the markout after its previous fills has been small.
Interviewer follow-up: is a skew on a £60m short a risk-reducing quote? It is risk-reducing if the skew is on the side that closes the short, and it costs spread on the side that increases it. Quantify both sides before choosing.

front: Describe what it means for a dealer to internalise a client trade, and name the three things the dealer can do with the residual risk after a client trade. Give the single number that decides between them.
back:
Internalise: the dealer takes the other side of the client's order into its own book, rather than passing it to an interdealer market or a venue.
Three choices for the residual: (1) warehouse it and carry the risk; (2) hedge it, either in the interdealer market or with futures or another instrument; (3) pass the risk on through a venue or a netting arrangement with another desk.
The decision number: the expected cost of holding the residual (its risk charge, plus the expected reversion value) against the cost of hedging it now (half-spread, market impact and fees). When the hedge cost is small relative to a day's risk, hedge; when it is large, warehouse only with a measured expected gain.
Interviewer follow-up: why does internalisation make the hit-ratio number harder to read? Because the dealer's inventory is part of the economics of every trade it fills, so the spread alone does not give the trade's value.

front: What is risk warehousing, and what must a desk believe to justify it? State the break-even condition in words and in one formula, using a hedge cost \(c\) per unit of DV01 and daily σ of the rate.
back:
Warehousing is carrying an unhedged residual position for a period in the expectation that it will be cheaper to hedge later, or that it earns a return while it is held.
Break-even: warehousing pays when the expected gain from waiting, \(\mathbb{E}[\text{gain}]\), exceeds the hedge cost \(c\) plus a risk charge for the period \(T\). Roughly, \(\mathbb{E}[\text{gain}] > c + \lambda\,\sigma_{day}\sqrt{T}\), where \(\lambda\) is the desk's price of risk per unit of 1σ, and \(\sigma\) is the rate's daily volatility in bp × DV01.
What must be true: a measured reversion or flow-netting value, a limit that allows the residual, and a plan to exit. A desk that cannot state the expected gain from waiting is taking a directional risk, not warehousing.
Interviewer follow-up: what is the break-even holding period for a hedge cost of £5k on £166k/bp? Set the risk charge equal to the hedge cost: \(\lambda\sqrt{T}\,\times\pounds830\text{k}=\pounds5\text{k}\), so \(\lambda\sqrt{T}\approx0.006\). A risk charge of 0.6% of 1σ per day gives a one-day break-even; a charge of 2% gives \(T\approx0.09\) days, about two hours.

front: How do desks tier clients for pricing, and which evidence moves a client from one tier to another? Give three metrics and say which one should carry the most weight.
back:
Three metrics:
  • Realised spread per unit DV01 traded, i.e. effective spread plus markout, measured over a rolling window. This is the economic measure.
  • Hit ratio and win-conditional markout, which show whether the client is price shopping and whether its wins are selected against you.
  • Franchise value: cross-product flow, balances, hedging activity and the value of the client relationship to the desk.
Weight: the realised spread per DV01 carries the most weight, because it is the only one that is a P&L number. Franchise value is real, but it should be a deliberate override with a stated rationale, not a default.
Noise: move a client only on a minimum sample and with a confidence interval on the mean realised spread. Otherwise you tier on a few large trades.
Interviewer follow-up: how do you avoid moving a client because of one event window? Exclude flagged event windows, then require the change to persist over at least two rolling windows.

front: Explain last look in an electronic dealer quote. Why does it matter to the client and to the dealer, and what does a desk measure to manage it?
back:
Mechanism: after the client hits a quote, the dealer has a short window in which it may reject the trade, usually when the market has moved against it.
Effect: the client's fill is a free option for the dealer. The option has value, and the price the dealer quotes absorbs part of that value.
Who cares: the client because its fills are not certain and its best quotes may be rejected exactly when they are most valuable. The dealer because it prevents adverse fills on stale quotes. Regulators and venues scrutinise last look, and the rules differ by market and by asset class, so check the current requirements for the venue in question.
What to measure: rejection rate by client and by size, the markout on accepted trades, and the markout on rejected trades (which shows the adverse flow the dealer avoided). A low rejection rate with a high accepted-trade markout means the quote is too tight for the flow.
Interviewer follow-up: does last look change the winner's curse? Yes, partly: rejections remove some adverse fills, so the accepted-trade markout understates the curse unless you look at rejected trades too.

front: A clearing-eligible, liquid interest rate swap is subject to a trading obligation in the UK and EU. What does that mean for where a dealer can execute it? Name the US analogue.
back:
Trading obligation: in-scope derivatives must be traded on a trading venue, meaning a regulated market, a multilateral trading facility (MTF) or an organised trading facility (OTF), unless an exemption applies. A bilateral trade outside a venue is not allowed for an in-scope class unless an exemption applies, and a systematic internaliser is not a trading venue.
Scope and exemptions: the list of in-scope classes and the exemptions are set by the regulator and change over time. Check the current list and the exemption conditions with compliance before relying on them.
US analogue: the swap execution facility (SEF) regime under Dodd-Frank. Certain swaps that are made available to trade must be executed on a SEF or a designated contract market, subject to the same kind of exemptions.
Desk impact: hedging executions, client-facing RFQs and block trades in in-scope classes need routing to the venue, and the venue choice affects the post-trade reporting and the TCA data you get.
Interviewer follow-up: is a dealer-to-dealer hedge in the same swap subject to the same obligation? Scope depends on the class and the counterparty, so answer by checking the class list, not by assuming it.

front: A streaming quoter updates its mid every 250ms. The mid's noise is roughly Brownian. What does the quoter need to widen when its feed is stale, and how does the cost scale with latency?
back:
Quantity at risk: the mid's 1σ move over a latency \(\tau\) is \(\sigma\sqrt{\tau}\). A stale quote can be picked off by a client who sees the move first, so the expected cost per fill is also proportional to \(\sigma\sqrt{\tau}\).
Scaling: cost scales with the square root of latency, not linearly. Ten times the latency costs about 3.2 times as much per fill.
What to widen: the half-spread should include \(k\,\sigma\sqrt{\tau}\) for the current feed age \(\tau\). The quoter should also cut size and, past a staleness timer, pull the quote.
Who gains: the quoter that is slower to update loses on the stale fills. A faster feed is worth paying for only when the stale-fill cost it saves exceeds its cost.
Interviewer follow-up: at what staleness should you pull a quote? When the expected stale-fill cost, \(\sigma\sqrt{\tau}/\sqrt{2\pi}\) times DV01 times the probability of a pick-off, exceeds the value of the fill.

front: On the Long Gilt future (£100,000 nominal), one tick of 0.01 per £100 is worth {{c1::£10}}.
back: Tick value = 0.01 / 100 × £100,000 = £10. The tick value is the minimum P&L per contract per tick, which sets the scale of hedge slippage.

front: On US 10-year note futures ($100,000 face), one tick of 1/64 is worth {{c1::$15.625}}.
A 1bp move in a 3-month SOFR future (on $1m face, 0.25-year accrual) is worth {{c1::$25}}.
For a dealer, realised spread = effective spread + {{c1::markout}}, where the markout is the dealer-side P&L move of the mid after the trade.
back: Example: effective 1.0bp, markout −1.5bp, realised −0.5bp. The sign convention is that a negative markout is adverse to the dealer.

front: A 1.0bp effective spread on £50m of 10y gilts at DV01 £40k/bp earns £{{c1::40,000}} at the trade. A 1.5bp adverse markout turns it into a realised £{{c2::−20,000}}.
back: 40,000 − 60,000 = −20,000. The markout (1.5bp × £40k = £60k) is larger than the spread earned, so the trade loses money after five minutes.
